feature.name: Cross-project dependency map
feature.description: Visualize blockers across teams with live links to tasks and Slack digests when critical paths slip. Spec: dependency-map-spec-v2.pdf. Product: FlowStack — team workflow hub connecting tasks, docs, and lightweight automations for growing product squads.

executiveSummary: FlowStack plans to ship a Cross-project dependency map (dependency-map-spec-v2.pdf) for B2B SaaS companies with 20–200 employees running multiple parallel initiatives, targeting Heads of Product / VPs of Engineering with a stated financial threshold of $180,000. The research run executed 11 planned tool calls, but only one produced data: a web_search_live query that returned 5 results, all of them vendor or third-party comparison/listicle content (monday.com blog x2, asana.com x1, a third-party blog x2). Without exception, the four intended competitor enrichment calls (Linear, Asana, Monday.com, Atlassian Jira) failed with identifier-format errors, and the company_search and both job_search calls failed with filter-format errors. Consequently, this report contains no firmographic data (employee counts, funding, ARR, tech stack), no buyer intent signals, and no market sizing — only directional qualitative signals from 5 comparison articles. The single usable signal: a monday.com-authored comparison states that Asana's "cross-project automation requires workarounds or third-party tools," which is the closest thing in the dataset to validation that cross-project dependency handling is an unaddressed pain in an adjacent incumbent. Recommended next step before committing the 14-week, 2-engineer build is to re-run the failed enrich/search steps with corrected parameters, since the current evidence base is insufficient to justify the investment against a 22-month runway and ~$180k/mo burn.

competitorLandscape.name: Asana
competitorLandscape.positioning: Presented in retrieved results as strong in portfolio management and rich in custom fields/templates, but weak on cross-project automation. No firmographic or pricing data was retrieved (enrich call failed).
relevantMoves: Maintains its own comparison/education content ('Best Project Management Software: 11 Tools Compared') that frames itself alongside Jira, Trello and monday.com — i.e., it competes on category ownership via content, not just product.
Per retrieved snippet, cross-project automation in Asana 'requires workarounds or third-party tools' — the primary documented opening for FlowStack's dependency map.
Listed as 'Strong in Portfolio Management' in a third-party 2026 tool comparison, indicating positioning one layer above task-level dependencies.

competitorLandscape.name: Monday.com
competitorLandscape.positioning: Presented as the top-ranked tool ('Our Winner') in third-party 2026 comparisons and as the publisher of competitive comparison content against Asana/Basecamp. No firmographic data retrieved (enrich call failed).
relevantMoves: Operates a high-volume project-management blog that publishes competitor comparisons (e.g., 'Asana vs Basecamp: 2026 comparison for teams'), a content-led acquisition play in exactly FlowStack's target segment.
Ranked #1 in an independent 2026 '10 Best Project Management Tools' list, indicating strong share of voice in the mid-market evaluation funnel where FlowStack would compete.
Positions itself as offering 'comprehensive agile project management capabilities' in comparison content alongside Jira and Asana.

competitorLandscape.name: Atlassian Jira
competitorLandscape.positioning: Appears in retrieved results as the tool 'tailored specifically for software' teams and as a default head-to-head against Asana in comparison content. No firmographic data, pricing, or roadmap data retrieved (identify/enrich calls failed).
relevantMoves: Occupies the 'software team default' position in third-party comparisons, meaning FlowStack's engineering-manager persona (Elena) and IC designer persona (Chris) most likely already live in Jira.
Third-party comparison content repeatedly pairs Jira and Asana as 'two leaders in project management,' implying the dependency-map feature must integrate with rather than replace Jira.
No retrieved evidence of a native cross-project dependency visualization move — this is an inference from absence, not a confirmed gap.

competitorLandscape.name: Linear
competitorLandscape.positioning: Not assessed. Linear was included in the research plan (company_identify and company_enrich) but both calls failed with identifier-format errors and Linear does not appear anywhere in the 5 retrieved web results.

marketSignals.signal: Cross-project automation is a documented weak point in a leading incumbent
marketSignals.evidence: Retrieved snippet: 'Asana: allows custom fields and templates, Cross-project automation requires workarounds or third-party tools.'
marketSignals.implicationForFeature: Directly supports the premise of the Cross-project dependency map: the pain is real enough that a competitor's own comparison page names it as an Asana limitation. FlowStack should lead positioning with 'no workarounds, no third-party glue.'

marketSignals.signal: Incumbents compete on portfolio-level framing, not dependency-level execution
marketSignals.evidence: Third-party 2026 comparison ranks 'Asana – Strong in Portfolio Management' above task-level capability discussion; Jira is framed as 'comprehensive agile project management capabilities tailored specifically for software.'
marketSignals.implicationForFeature: Leaves the operational layer — what my squad owes other teams before sprint planning (persona Elena) — less explicitly claimed by incumbents, a plausible wedge for a focused dependency map aimed at 20–200 employee squads rather than enterprises.

marketSignals.signal: Category discovery is funneled through vendor-authored 'best tool' listicles
marketSignals.evidence: Of 5 retrieved results, 2 are published on monday.com's own blog and 1 on asana.com's own site; the monday.com-authored set includes an 'Asana vs Basecamp' comparison and a listicle in which a third party names monday.com the winner.
marketSignals.implicationForFeature: FlowStack's buyer research is being mediated by competitors' content. The dependency map needs a comparison-proof claim (e.g., explicit cross-project/Slack digest capability) or FlowStack will be evaluated, and dismissed, on incumbents' framing.

marketSignals.signal: The comparison content is denser on setup/onboarding time than on dependency capability
marketSignals.evidence: Retrieved snippet references implementation effort: 'Asana: Takes two to four weeks…' in the context of a team-tool comparison.
marketSignals.implicationForFeature: Setup friction is a live evaluation criterion in this segment, which aligns with the new-install persona (Alicia, new PM at a Series A inheriting a messy roadmap). The dependency map should be demonstrably usable on day one without a migration project.

marketSignals.signal: No feature-specific evidence surfaced for 'cross-project dependency mapping' as a category
marketSignals.evidence: The single successful search — 'cross-project dependency mapping tools B2B SaaS mid-market 2025 Linear Asana Monday.com Jira' — returned only 5 generic project-management comparison articles; none addressed dependency mapping as a distinct capability or category.
marketSignals.implicationForFeature: Cannot be read as proof the category is empty; it is equally consistent with weak query coverage. Treat as a hypothesis to test with corrected search parameters before sizing the opportunity.

gapsAndOpportunities: Named gap in an adjacent incumbent: cross-project automation in Asana 'requires workarounds or third-party tools' (monday.com comparison page) — FlowStack can position the dependency map as removing third-party glue and manual workarounds.

Dependency visibility is framed by incumbents at portfolio level; the day-to-day question for the engineering-manager persona (Elena) — 'what does my squad owe other teams before sprint planning' — is not explicitly claimed in any retrieved content.

Onboarding friction ('two to four weeks' reference in comparison content) is an explicit evaluation criterion, creating an opening for a dependency map that works immediately for a new PM inheriting a messy roadmap (Alicia persona).

Slack digest alerting on critical-path slips is a distribution and stickiness opportunity: it inserts FlowStack into the daily channel where the designer persona (Chris) already waits for unblock notifications, rather than requiring a new tool-checking habit.

The 20–200 employee mid-market segment is described in FlowStack's own targeting as running multiple parallel initiatives; retrieved comparison content is oriented to either generic SMB or enterprise-portfolio framing, leaving a middle-band positioning surface — though this gap is asserted from FlowStack's brief, not verified by retrieved data.

Vendor-dominated comparison content (monday.com and asana.com publish their own listicles) indicates FlowStack cannot win discovery passively and should plan a comparison/positioning asset alongside the feature launch.
risks: Evidence base is critically thin: 10 of 11 planned research steps failed, leaving only 5 web results — all vendor-authored or third-party listicles — as the entire external input to this report.

No competitor firmographics were retrieved (employee count, funding, tech stack, estimated ARR all failed for Linear, Asana, Monday.com and Atlassian), so no assessment can be made of relative R&D capacity or likelihood of a fast-follow.
No market sizing or demand quantification was produced (company_search failed with a filter-format error), so the 20–200 employee / US-EU mid-market opportunity is unvalidated by data.
No hiring or roadmap signals were captured (both job_search calls failed), removing the best available proxy for whether competitors are staffing up on dependency/automation work.

Linear received zero coverage in retrieved results, meaning the most product-culture-adjacent competitor in the set is entirely unassessed — a blind spot for a feature aimed at software product squads.

Feature is plausibly replicable by incumbents: the one documented gap is described as a limitation incumbents currently accept, not one they cannot address, and the map/digest concept is a surface-level layer on data incumbents already hold.

Integration dependence on Jira, Slack and Notion APIs is implied by FlowStack's own positioning ('connects tasks, docs, and lightweight automations') and by retrieved signals that Jira is the software-team default; partner API changes or access restrictions would directly degrade the Slack-digest and live-task-link promise.

Cost and runway pressure: the feature consumes 2 full-stack engineers for 14 weeks plus ~$3k/mo extra graph/alerting infra during beta, against ~$1.8M ARR, ~72% gross margin, ~$180k/mo EBITDA burn and 22 months of runway — a meaningful commitment to an evidence base this weak.

Two of three named personas (Elena, Sam) solve for planning rituals already served by Jira/Notion, so the feature risks being perceived as an additional dashboard rather than a replacement for an existing workflow.
Financial threshold of $180,000 used in the plan cannot be validated against any retrieved pricing or deal-size data; no buyer-budget evidence was collected in this run.

Source bias: half of retrieved results are published by a direct competitor (monday.com), including the single quoted claim about Asana's cross-project limitation — that claim is self-serving and should be verified independently before it is used in positioning.
dataLimitations: company_identify failed for all 4 targets (Linear, Asana, Monday.com, Atlassian Jira) with 'Exactly one identifier must be provided' — no company identities were resolved.

company_enrich failed for all 3 attempted domains (linear.app, asana.com, monday.com) with the same identifier-format error — no employee counts, industries, locations, funding, tech stack, descriptions or estimated ARR were obtained.
company_search failed ('filters' must be a single condition or a tree) — no list of 20–200 employee US/EU B2B SaaS companies was produced, despite a planned limit of 50.

Both job_search calls failed with the same filter-format error — no Product Operations or Engineering Manager job data, and no competitor hiring signals for dependency mapping, cross-project dependencies or workflow automation.
Only 1 of 11 planned steps returned any data (web_search_live), yielding 5 results, all of which are comparison/listicle articles rather than feature-specific, buyer, or pricing sources.

No retrieved source addresses 'cross-project dependency mapping' as a named capability; the feature's competitive differentiation is inferred from a single third-party-hosted quote about Asana and from absence of contrary evidence.
No pricing, packaging, or contract-value data was retrieved for any competitor; the $180,000 financial threshold in the plan is an internally supplied figure, not a validated market input.
No geography-specific evidence: the plan targets US and EU, but retrieved sources are English-language vendor blogs with no EU-specific regulatory, localization, or buying-behavior data.

No primary research was conducted in this run; user interview material (flowstack-user-interviews-summary.pdf) and the feature spec (dependency-map-spec-v2.pdf) were supplied as inputs but were not independently verified against external evidence.

All retrieved articles are dated between Sept 2025 and Feb 2026, and the search execution timestamp (1791789725392 ms) precedes the latest article date, indicating recency claims should be treated cautiously.
No quantitative market signals were collected (TAM/SAM, growth rates, win/loss, churn, adoption) — every marketSignal in this report is qualitative and directional only.
